[[Image:Dr Ingrid N Visser - by Jo Berghan-HPF.jpg|thumb|Ingrid Visser]]

'''Ingrid Natasha Visser''' (born 20 February 1966)is a New Zealand conservation activist<ref>{{Cite web |last=Parque |first=Loro |date=2017-10-11 |title=Loro Parque en redes |url=https://www.loroparque.com/en/ingrid-visser-and-rosina-liske/ |access-date=2026-09-16 |website=Loro Parque |language=en-US}}</ref> and public figure known for campaigning on issues involving [[Orca|orcas]] and [[marine mammal]] protection<ref>{{Cite web |title=Orca Captivity |url=https://www.orcaresearch.org/orca-captivity/ |access-date=2026-09-16 |website=Orca Research Trust |language=en-US}}</ref>. She is also a marine biologist with a PhD from the [[University of Auckland]] and founded the Orca Research Trust.

== Early life ==
Visser was born in [[Lower Hutt]], [[Wellington]], New Zealand. Her parents were Dutch immigrants who moved to New Zealand in the 1950s.  They were both nationalised as New Zealanders after she was born.{{Citation needed|date=February 2022}}

Between June 1982 and November 1986, Visser sailed with her parents and sister aboard a {{convert|17|metres|feet|adj=on}} yacht around the world.<ref>{{cite news |url= http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10692370 |title=New Zealander of the Year Finalist: Dr Ingrid Visser |author=Geoff Cumming |date=6 December 2010 |publisher=New Zealand Herald }}</ref> The trip covered over {{convert|50000|nmi|km}} and visited more than 40 countries.

== Education ==
Visser holds three university degrees: a Bachelor of Science ([[Massey University]]), a Masters of Science, and a Doctorate of Philosophy (both [[University of Auckland|the University of Auckland]]).  Visser has been working with orca (''[[Orcinus orca]]'', also known as killer whales) since 1992 and completed her PhD in 2000,<ref>{{cite thesis |last=Visser |first=Ingrid |year=2000 |type=Doctoral thesis |title=Orca (Orcinus orca) in New Zealand waters |publisher=ResearchSpace@Auckland, University of Auckland |hdl=2292/614 |url=https://researchspace.auckland.ac.nz/handle/2292/614}}</ref> the first scientific study of orca in New Zealand waters.

== Scientific work ==
[[File:Woman swims with killer whales in the wild.webm|thumb|Visser's team with wild orca]]
Her research on orca has been published in international scientific journals, since 1998, and many of these publications are available on the Orca Research Trust website.<ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.orcaresearch.org/index.php/scientific-articles| title=Scientific Articles| publisher=Orca Research Trust}}</ref>

In 2002 Visser's research was instrumental in the New Zealand Government's reclassification of New Zealand orcas from "Common" in the New Zealand Threat Classification System to "Nationally Critical".  This is the equivalent status of "Critically Endangered" in the internationally recognised [[IUCN]] Red Data listing.

While her earlier research focused on New Zealand orca populations, her more recent work has included expedition-based guiding and lecturing.

Although some of her publications are recent, they have included analyses of data and observations collected during earlier field studies. Her most recent publication on New Zealand Orca was based on data collected in 2014<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Loch |first1=Carolina |last2=Visser |first2=Ingrid N. |last3=Stratford |first3=Kali |last4=White |first4=Sophie |last5=Wakefield |first5=Joe |last6=Bull |first6=Stewart |last7=Matenga |first7=Lydia |last8=Johnstone |first8=Muriel |last9=Oliphant-Stewart |first9=Ramari |date=2025-12-01 |title=Tooth wear and dental calculus in a group of orca (Orcinus orca) stranded on the New Zealand southern coast |url=https://doi.org/10.1080/03036758.2025.2491510 |journal=Journal of the Royal Society of New Zealand |publisher=Taylor & Francis |volume=55 |issue=6 |pages=2042–2059 |doi=10.1080/03036758.2025.2491510 |issn=0303-6758 |pmc=12315212 |pmid=40756860 |bibcode=2025JRSNZ..55.2042L }}</ref>

Publicly available DOC records identify marine-mammal permits held by Visser, including a permit for leopard-seal research recorded as active from 2018 to 2028.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Aotea Conservation Park Advisory Committee |url=https://ftp.doc.govt.nz/public/folder/oOkRQMxqEUKNepX4kTZWbg/aotea-conservation-park-advisory-committee/meeting-agendas/ACPAC-20181210-Agenda-10-Dec-2018.pdf}}</ref>However, the current status and expiry date of the separate permit or authorisation associated with her New Zealand orca research are not clear from the publicly available records located.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Loch |first1=Carolina |last2=Visser |first2=Ingrid |last3=Stratford |first3=Kali |last4=White |first4=Sophie |last5=Wakefield |first5=Joe |last6=Bull |first6=Stewart |last7=Matenga |first7=Lydia |last8=Johnstone |first8=Muriel |last9=Stewart |first9=Ramari |date=2025-05-06 |title=Tooth wear and dental calculus in a group of orca ( Orcinus orca ) stranded on the New Zealand southern coast |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/391489336 |journal=Journal of the Royal Society of New Zealand |volume=55 |issue=6 |pages=2042–2059 |doi=10.1080/03036758.2025.2491510 |pmid=40756860 |pmc=12315212 |bibcode=2025JRSNZ..55.2042L }}</ref>

Visser’s research methods and professional conduct have also attracted criticism.<ref>{{Cite web |title=New Zealander of the Year Finalist: Dr Ingrid Visser |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/new-zealander-of-the-year-finalist-dr-ingrid-visser/A4BZ6JABGOKSHAG5EUYOOMO3GM/ |access-date=2026-09-15 |website=NZ Herald |language=en-NZ}}</ref>Her practice of habituating wild orca and engaging in close interactions with them has raised concerns about whether her presence may influence the animals’ behaviour and affect the objectivity of behavioural observations.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Marino |first1=Lori |last2=Frohoff |first2=Toni |date=2011 |title=Towards a new paradigm of non-captive research on cetacean cognition |journal=PLOS ONE |volume=6 |issue=9 |article-number=e24121 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0024121  |doi-access=free|issn=1932-6203 |pmc=3168481 |pmid=21915286 |bibcode=2011PLoSO...624121M }}</ref>Some of her public claims are based on personal observations, photographs, or unpublished data, which can make independent assessment and replication difficult.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Massey News Archieve 2006 |url=https://www.massey.ac.nz/about/news/massey-news-archive/}}</ref> 

In a separate resource-consent process, marine scientist David Clement noted that a species-status table submitted by Visser relied on older conservation references than those used in his assessment, resulting in differences between the two evaluations. Her work also encompasses advocacy publications, conference posters, expert reports, and legal submissions in addition to peer-reviewed scientific research.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Statement of evidence of Deanna Marie Clement: Potential effects of proposed Northport reclamation on marine mammals |url=https://www.nrc.govt.nz/media/txkl254o/d-clement-evidence-marine-mammals.pdf |website=Northland Regional Council |date=24 August 2023}}</ref>

== Publications ==
She has published numerous popular articles and her photographs have appeared in magazines such as [[National Geographic (magazine)|''National Geographic'']], [[BBC Wildlife]], ''[[New Zealand Geographic]]'', and ''[[An Encyclopedia of New Zealand]]''.<ref>{{Cite encyclopedia |url= http://www.teara.govt.nz/en/photograph/4014/ingrid-visser-scientist |title=Orcas – Feeding and other habits| encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of New Zealand| publisher=Te Ara| first=Gerard| last=Hutching| date=9 July 2013}}</ref>

Visser has set up the Orca Research Trust, the Antarctic Killer Whale Identification Catalogue.

Visser has written an [[autobiography]], ''Swimming with Orca'', which was a finalist in the Environmental category of the New Zealand [[Montana Book Awards]], and two children's books (''I Love Killer Whales'' and ''The Orca'').  The latter has been translated into [[Māori language|Māori]] and is currently in press as a bilingual English/Spanish publication.

== Other work ==
{{outdated|2017's proposed bill|date=April 2026}}
Visser is a member of the Australia & New Zealand branch of [[The Explorers Club]] and continues to travel the world in search of orca.  She published the first manuscript on [[Papua New Guinea]] orca, and returns regularly to [[Walindi Plantation Resort]] to conduct field research there.

She serves as [[Chairman|Chair]] of the Free Morgan Foundation, an organization involved in efforts to free captive orca [[Morgan (orca)|Morgan]] in Europe, and has appeared in court in relation to those efforts.<ref>{{Cite web| url=http://www.freemorgan.org/| title=Free Morgan Foundation| work=freemorgan.org| publisher=Free Morgan| accessdate=21 October 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite web| title=Dr. Visser says park suing her over report submitted in court| url=http://www.digitaljournal.com/article/338491| author=Elizabeth Batt| publisher=Digital Journal| date=10 December 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201112013222/http://www.digitaljournal.com/article/338491|archive-date=12 November 2020}}</ref>

In September 2010, she co-founded Whale Rescue, an organisation of volunteers who provide logistical and practical expertise and equipment for rescuing [[cetaceans]].

In June 2017, she served as a witness to a Senate committee on Fisheries and Oceans in the Senate of Canada in favour of Bill S-203, which would make it illegal to keep cetaceans and whales in captivity in Canada.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://sencanada.ca/en/Committees/POFO/NoticeOfMeeting/455674/|title=Senate of Canada|date=1 June 2017|access-date=26 August 2017}}</ref>

Visser has been involved in the rescue and attempted rehabilitation of stranded orca calves in New Zealand. In 2016, she participated in the response to a young orca calf, known as “Bob” or “Tama”, in Tauranga Harbour. In 2021, Visser was also involved in the care of Toa, an unweaned orca calf stranded near Plimmerton.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Parque |first=Loro |date=2021-08-20 |title=Loro Parque en redes |url=https://www.loroparque.com/en/a-tale-of-two-rescues-how-experience-and-resources-derived-from-marine-mammal-facilities-drives-success-in-whale-stranding-operations/ |access-date=2026-09-15 |website=Loro Parque |language=en-US}}</ref>

Her handling of both cases attracted scrutiny<ref>{{Cite web |title=Orca incident Plimmerton – technical notes and advice |url=https://www.doc.govt.nz/news/oia-responses/2021/}}</ref>, particularly over the decision to hold the calves in human care and the extent to which the interventions aligned with advice from the Department of Conservation (DOC). In the Tauranga case, DOC records indicated that the intervention differed from the department’s traditional approach to marine-mammal strandings. In the case of Toa, DOC considered euthanasia among the possible options, while Visser advocated continued rehabilitation and attempts to reunite the calf with its pod.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-08-09 |title=SunLive - Orca incident outside normal protocols - The Bay's News First |url=https://www.sunlive.co.nz/news/132797-orca-incident-outside-normal-protocols.html |access-date=2026-09-15 |website=www.sunlive.co.nz |language=en}}</ref> Critics have questioned whether the interventions were appropriately justified and managed, particularly given that both calves died while in human care.
